verdict_reasoning: Level 1b fails on demand-1. The thread names no workload that spends time on ckpt_lck, message #10 says contention was not measured, and message #13 expects no performance effect from v2. The lock is taken a few times per checkpoint request, so the new lock-free protocol carries ordering risk with no stated gain. The level 2 objection replication-ondisk-1 survived but was not evaluated because of the base-up rule.

brief.title: Replace spinlocks around single-field reads and writes with barriers or atomics
brief.problem: The author sees many places where a spinlock guards a single load or store of a shared field, and calls this unnecessary locking. The thread names no workload or user who suffers from it. The author did not measure contention and expects the v2 checkpointer change to have no performance effect.
brief.proposed_design: v1 added slock_read_*/slock_write_* helpers in spin.h, first using barriers and then pg_atomic membarrier calls for 32- and 64-bit fields, and replaced lock-protected accesses in 20 files. After objections, v2 narrows the change to checkpointer.c. It removes ckpt_lck and packs ckpt_flags with a version number into one pg_atomic_uint32, using memory barriers and race detection for the counters.
user_visible_surface: v1: new C helpers slock_read_<type> and slock_write_<type> in storage/spin.h, generated by SLOCK_DEFINE_SCALAR_ACCESSORS.
v2: CheckpointerShmem loses ckpt_lck; src/include/access/xlog.h changes, with no detail on what.
v2: RequestCheckpoint can report a different error message when a checkpoint that started before the request fails.
author_claims: About 105 places in 26 files take a spinlock only around one access.
A read of CurrBytePos without insertpos_lck sees either the value before or after the update, so it is safe.
RequestCheckpoint with CHECKPOINT_WAIT already reports failures of unrelated checkpoints, which makes the lock-free design simpler.
The author expects no performance impact from v2 but thinks it is still useful.
brief.thread_state: Andres Freund called the v1 mechanical replacement dangerous and the write-side changes wrong, and asked for one conversion at a time with analysis documented in code; Merlin Moncure showed a broken xlog.c case. v2 for the checkpointer has no replies yet.
unclear: What benefit v2 brings if it does not improve performance.
Whether v2 documents the new memory-ordering rules in code comments, as Andres Freund asked.
Whether v1 is withdrawn or still proposed for the other files.
How the version-number scheme handles the race between REQUEST and STARTED on weakly ordered platforms.

prior_attempts.title: fix spinlock contention in LogwrtResult
prior_attempts.quote: I realized that because of commit e369f3708636 this change is no longer as critical as it used to be, so I'm withdrawing this patch from the commitfest.
prior_attempts.reason: The author withdrew the patch himself. In April 2022 he held it back from that cycle because the memory barrier needs were hard to get right and he did not want subtle bugs in WAL. In September 2022 he withdrew it because commit e369f3708636 made the change less critical.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1 targeted a contended lock, info_lck on LogwrtResult, and converted its fields to 64-bit atomics. v2 here targets ckpt_lck, with no contention claim and no expected performance effect.

prior_attempts.title: Move PinBuffer and UnpinBuffer to atomics
prior_attempts.quote: Which you made ineffective because PinBuffer() doesn't take a lock anymore. Mutual exclusion through locks only works if all participants take the locks.
prior_attempts.reason: Andres Freund judged the first patch incorrect. PinBuffer no longer took the header lock, but StrategyGetBuffer, SyncOneBuffer and BufferAlloc still relied on that lock for mutual exclusion. Work moved to the single atomic state version, which Alexander Korotkov refactored and others benchmarked, and it was still being cleaned up when the entry closed. No visible message states why the entry was returned.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P7 removed the lock on one side while other paths still relied on it, which matches the objection to v1 writes in message #8. v2 removes ckpt_lck from all participants, so that reason does not apply to v2.

objections.title: No measured contention or user problem justifies lock-free conversion
objections.failure_scenario: A committer pushes the lock-free checkpointer protocol to gain nothing measurable. Later, a memory-ordering bug on ARM or POWER makes RequestCheckpoint with CHECKPOINT_WAIT return early or report the wrong failure. Users find out from an unexplained checkpoint error or a backup that did not wait.
objections.argument: The thread names no workload, user report or benchmark where these spinlocks cost anything. In message #10 the author says contention was not measured, and in message #13 expects v2 to have no performance effect. The checkpointer locks are taken a few times per checkpoint, which is a cold path. Every user carries the risk of subtle ordering bugs, as message #8 warns, while nobody is shown to gain. [P1] pulled a similar atomics change for the same mix of hard barrier rules and reduced need.
objections.author_must_show: Which workload shows measurable time spent on ckpt_lck or on another spinlock you plan to convert, and how much does the change recover?

critic.reasoning: Message #10 says contention was not measured, and message #13 expects no performance effect from v2 and names no other benefit. [P1] concerned a contended lock, so it supports only the point that barrier rules are hard.

other_surviving.title: Lock-free RequestCheckpoint wait must still cover the request
other_surviving.failure_scenario: On a weakly ordered machine, a backend running CREATE DATABASE with FILE_COPY, DROP DATABASE or pg_backup_start calls RequestCheckpoint with CHECKPOINT_WAIT. It misses the STARTED increment and returns after a checkpoint that began before its flags were seen, so it proceeds as if its changes were already on disk. A later crash or a standby replay exposes missing or stale relation files.
other_surviving.argument: Callers rely on one invariant: a CHECKPOINT_WAIT return means a checkpoint that began after the request has finished, and that checkpoint carries the request's flags. v2 removes ckpt_lck, drops the ckpt_done update on FAILED, and handles the REQUEST/STARTED race with a version number packed next to ckpt_flags. The commit message gives this race one sentence and no memory-ordering argument, and the thread does not show that v2 puts the rules in code comments as message #12 asks. Andres Freund warned in message #8 that reads may depend on fields updated together under the lock, and that applies here.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What argument, written in checkpointer.c, shows that a CHECKPOINT_WAIT caller on ARM or POWER never returns before a checkpoint that saw its flags has completed?

precedents.title: Move PinBuffer and UnpinBuffer to atomics

critic.reasoning: The v2 commit message gives the REQUEST/STARTED race one sentence and no ordering argument for weakly ordered platforms. CHECKPOINT_WAIT callers depend on that guarantee, and message #12 asks for the rules in code comments.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: Lock-free checkpointer protocol with no claimed benefit repeats a withdrawn tradeoff
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer pushes v2 and later a fix lands in RequestCheckpoint or CheckpointerMain. On a weakly ordered platform, CHECKPOINT with CHECKPOINT_WAIT then returns before its checkpoint, or reports a false failure. The bug shows up only under rare races, long after commit, and nobody gained performance in exchange.
refuted.argument: In [P1], a spinlock-to-atomics conversion in xlog.c was held back because the memory-barrier needs were hard to get right, then withdrawn once the gain became less critical. That record is an AI summary, so it is a pointer only. v2 has the same shape: a new ordering protocol, here a version number packed with ckpt_flags plus race detection on ckpt_started, while message #13 expects no performance effect. Message #12 asks for a high payoff, and v2 does not yet state one.
refuted.author_must_show: What measurable gain or simplification does removing ckpt_lck give that justifies a new lock-free protocol in RequestCheckpoint, and where do the code comments document its ordering rules?

precedents.title: Replace spinlock with lwlock in pg_stat_statements

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1, which makes the same point about a new ordering protocol with no stated gain. [P2] is about replacing a spinlock with an LWLock and does not support this objection.

refuted.title: Lock-free checkpointer state adds ordering rules with no measured gain
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch adds a field or a step to the checkpoint request protocol and reads it next to ckpt_started with plain loads. On weakly ordered hardware a backend waiting with CHECKPOINT_WAIT then misses a start or reports a stale failure. Nobody sees it until a rare hang or a false error shows up in the field.
refuted.argument: ckpt_lck is taken a few times per checkpoint request, a cold path, and message #13 expects no performance effect from v2. The patch replaces an obvious lock with a version-number race-detection scheme that every future editor of checkpointer.c must understand. Message #12 sets the bar that the payoff must justify the review cost, and message #10 shows contention was never measured. [P1] (AI summary) shows a similar conversion held back because the barrier needs were hard to get right for the benefit.
refuted.author_must_show: Which workload takes ckpt_lck often enough to matter, and what measured gain justifies the new memory-ordering rules in checkpointer.c?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1. A stated benefit or a simpler design in a new version could answer it, so the severity would be fixable in any case.

refuted.title: Packing CHECKPOINT_* flags with a version number limits future flags
refuted.failure_scenario: A developer adds a new CHECKPOINT_* bit in xlog.h, as has been done before. The bit takes space from the version counter, or overlaps it, and nothing fails at compile time. The version wraps sooner, and RequestCheckpoint misjudges whether the checkpointer saw its flags.
refuted.argument: The commit message says the flags and a version number share one pg_atomic_uint32 and that xlog.h changes, but it gives no bit layout. It also does not say how version wraparound is handled. The flag set is used outside checkpointer.c, so the packing couples an unrelated header to a private protocol. The proposal shows no static assertion or comment that would warn the next editor.
refuted.author_must_show: How many bits does the version get, what fails at build time when a new flag would collide with it, and why is wraparound harmless?

critic.reasoning: The scenario assumes that no mask or static assertion exists, but the code is not shown and v2 does touch xlog.h. A wraparound failure would need the version to wrap inside one request window, and the objection gives no path to that.

refuted.title: No one familiar with the checkpointer has engaged with v2
refuted.failure_scenario: v2 is committed with a subtle ordering bug that appears only on ARM or POWER under concurrent CHECKPOINT calls. The author has said he does not know the checkpointer well, and the reviewer he hoped for has limited his time. The fix then falls to a committer who never reviewed the design.
refuted.argument: In message #13 the author says he does not know the checkpointer as a whole and inferred the logic from the code. In message #12 Andres Freund says he will look some but cannot review many rounds. v2 has no replies. The CommitFest entry also does not say whether the 20-file v1 is withdrawn, which leaves reviewers unsure of the scope.
refuted.author_must_show: Is v1 withdrawn, and which reviewer familiar with checkpointer.c and the barrier rules has agreed to check the v2 protocol?

critic.reasoning: Andres Freund, a committer who knows this area, engaged in messages #2, #8 and #12 and offered limited review. v2 follows his advice to post one conversion with analysis, and the author answered every reply, so this is a committability note.

refuted.title: slock_* helpers duplicate the existing pg_atomic membarrier API
refuted.failure_scenario: A developer later finds a field read with slock_read_uint64(&lock, &field) and written elsewhere under SpinLockAcquire(&lock) with other fields. The lock argument is ignored, but the call looks locked, so the developer assumes the read is protected. A torn multi-field read, like the CurrBytePos case in message #9, goes unnoticed until a weak-memory platform shows it.
refuted.argument: Postgres already has pg_atomic_uint32/uint64 with pg_atomic_read_membarrier_* and pg_atomic_write_membarrier_*, which shihao pointed to in message #5. v1.1 builds on those calls but wraps them in spinlock-named helpers that take a slock_t and ignore it (message #7). In message #10 the author argues the name signals that a lock guards the variable. Andres answered in messages #8 and #12 that the state should become independent of the spinlock, and the material does not show whether v1 is withdrawn.
refuted.author_must_show: Is v1's slock_* API withdrawn, and if not, what can it express that a pg_atomic field with membarrier accessors and a code comment cannot?

critic.reasoning: Andres Freund raised this point in messages #8 and #12. v2 touches only checkpointer.c and xlog.h, not spin.h, and uses a pg_atomic_uint32 directly, so the current patch does not carry the slock_* helpers.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: v2 changes how RequestCheckpoint with CHECKPOINT_WAIT detects that its checkpoint finished, and callers rely on that for durability.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: v2 changes src/include/access/xlog.h without saying how; v1 adds slock_* helpers to storage/spin.h.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: v1 touches lwlock.c, freelist.c and xlog.c; v2 touches only the checkpoint request path, which is cold.

Which workload shows measurable time spent on ckpt_lck or on another spinlock you plan to convert, and how much does the change recover?
What argument, written in checkpointer.c, shows that a CHECKPOINT_WAIT caller on ARM or POWER never returns before a checkpoint that saw its flags has completed?
Is the 20-file v1 series withdrawn, or is it still proposed for the files other than checkpointer.c?

committability.owner_note: Andres Freund replied in messages #2, #8 and #12 but said he cannot review many rounds, and v2 has no replies. The owner must know checkpointer.c and the memory-barrier rules on weakly ordered platforms.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the CHECKPOINT_WAIT guarantee under a lock-free protocol on every supported platform, with no end date. Ordering bugs of this kind appear only under rare races.

precedents_retrieved.title: fix spinlock contention in LogwrtResult
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes contention on XLogCtl's info_lck spinlock, which backends take often to read LogwrtResult. The first version added an LWLock covering LogwrtResult and LogwrtRqst; later versions turned the shared LogwrtResult fields into 64-bit atomics, as Andres Freund suggested.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch himself. In April 2022 he held it back from that cycle because the memory barrier needs were hard to get right and he did not want subtle bugs in WAL. In September 2022 he withdrew it because commit e369f3708636 made the change less critical.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I realized that because of commit e369f3708636 this change is no longer
as critical as it used to be, so I'm withdrawing this patch from the
commitfest.

precedents_retrieved.title: Replace spinlock with lwlock in pg_stat_statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch (pgss_lwlock) replaces the per-entry spinlock in pg_stat_statements with an LWLock, to reduce contention in pgss_store() that track_planning made worse. The benchmark that motivated it showed about a 45% TPS drop at 128 or more connections in a fully-cached pgbench select-only test on v13beta1.
precedents_retrieved.objection: A benchmark by bttanakahbk showed no gain from the patch and a drop of more than 50% in TPS with a "SELECT 1;" workload, regardless of track_planning. The author, Fujii Masao, then concluded that replacing the spinlock with an LWLock is not the right approach. Alternatives (two spinlocks per entry, atomics for the counters) were discussed but not built. Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with Feedback because the discussion had stalled and the patch was incorrect.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improve documentation for spinlocks file
precedents_retrieved.objectors: David Fetter, Tom Lane, Robert Haas
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds comments to s_lock.h that list the current platform-specific spinlock implementations, as a guide for future contributors. A revised version added a "File layout" block comment and "Currently implemented" lines in each section.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers said such comments are not tied to the code they describe, so they become obsolete when someone changes or adds a platform implementation without updating them. Tom Lane also said platform details do not belong in the header's macro specification. Robert Haas found the revised layout and "Currently implemented" comments redundant with the code and saw little point to the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
As Tom basically said before, I think the "File layout" block
comment will just get out of date and be a maintenance annoyance to
future updaters of this file.

precedents_retrieved.title: Atomic rename feature for Windows
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes pgrename() on Windows use SetFileInformationByHandle with FILE_RENAME_FLAG_POSIX_SEMANTICS, so a rename can replace a file that is still open, as on POSIX. It raised _WIN32_WINNT to Windows 10 and added a manifest so IsWindows10OrGreater() works; a later version used the feature only on Windows build 17763 and up.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry closed because Thomas Munro rebased and simplified the patch and moved the work to a new thread and CommitFest entry. Earlier review had objected to raising the minimum Windows version and to the extra manifest files. Thomas Munro's open questions were behavior on non-NTFS filesystems and whether to require POSIX rename, since the non-POSIX fallback would likely go untested.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
As Thomas has incorporated this patch into another CommitFest entry
[1], we'll close
the entry for this thread [2].

precedents_retrieved.title: Atomic pgrename on Windows
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Andres Freund, Magnus Hagander, David Steele
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch made pgrename() on Windows replace the target file atomically, even when another process has it open, by calling ReplaceFile() when the target exists and MoveFileEx() otherwise. It aimed to fix "Permission denied" errors seen when renaming the statistics temp file on loaded Windows servers.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers questioned the approach. Andres Freund asked why opening files with FILE_SHARE_DELETE does not already prevent the error, and suggested retry logic instead. Magnus Hagander proposed trying MoveFileEx() first and falling back to ReplaceFile() on a sharing violation, possibly with a retry loop. The commitfest manager marked it Returned with Feedback because a new patch was needed, and the author agreed both approaches still had to be implemented and tested.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Even so, it looks like the approach needs a rethink so better to wait for that.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix typo 586/686 in atomics/arch-x86.h
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes misspelled macros in src/include/port/atomics/arch-x86.h, where `__i568__` and `__i668__` should be `__i586__` and `__i686__`. These checks select the x86 code paths for 8-byte atomic operations on 32-bit gcc builds.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers suggested removing the broken checks rather than fixing them, since no one had complained since 2017. Andres Freund is quoted saying the 32-bit special handling should be dropped instead of fixing the typos, and the author then returned the patch himself. His follow-up idea to drop 32-bit support entirely was opposed by Tom Lane, Nathan Bossart and Andres Freund.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: That indeed looks like a clear typo, but if noone has complained since 2017 then maybe removing the checks is the right course of action?

precedents_retrieved.title: Move PinBuffer and UnpinBuffer to atomics
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch made the buffer descriptor fields refcount and usage_count atomic, so PinBuffer and UnpinBuffer no longer take the buffer header spinlock. Later in the thread it was replaced by a version from Andres Freund that packs flags, usage_count and refcount into one 32-bit atomic state, with a BM_LOCKED flag acting as the header lock.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund judged the first patch incorrect. PinBuffer no longer took the header lock, but StrategyGetBuffer, SyncOneBuffer and BufferAlloc still relied on that lock for mutual exclusion. Work moved to the single atomic state version, which Alexander Korotkov refactored and others benchmarked, and it was still being cleaned up when the entry closed. No visible message states why the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Which you made ineffective because PinBuffer() doesn't take a lock
anymore. Mutual exclusion through locks only works if all participants
take the locks.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow reads to proceed during FK/trigger drops by reducing relation-level lock from AccessExclusive to ShareRowExclusive
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lowers the relation-level lock taken while dropping foreign key constraints and their RI triggers from AccessExclusiveLock to ShareRowExclusiveLock, so that SELECTs on the other table keep running. A revised patch narrowed the change to RI action triggers on the referenced table and kept AccessExclusiveLock elsewhere.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane said the change is unsafe for FK removal, because the planner may have built query plans that rely on the constraint holding, as the comment in AlterTableGetLockLevel explains. He also noted that the first patch lowered the lock for other constraint types, and that dropping a unique constraint can also break existing plans. The author posted a narrower patch, but no one replied to it, and the visible messages do not show why it was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Adding a foreign key can (and I think does) take a lesser lock,
because the additional constraint won't invalidate any proofs the
optimizer may have made beforehand.  But dropping one seems
problematic.

roaster_notes.note: v1's mechanical replacement was settled as wrong in messages #8 and #12, so I raise nothing on v1. The one objection concerns v2 only.

Within the standards and compatibility angle, nothing here supports an objection: there is no new SQL syntax, keyword, GUC, catalog object, psql change or pg_dump impact. The only user-visible effect is that CHECKPOINT may report a slightly different error message in a failure case, and error text is not a compatibility contract. The xlog.h change is not described. If it changes the CHECKPOINT_* flag values or how many bits they may use, extensions that call RequestCheckpoint would be affected, but that cannot be checked from the material and is an internal API concern.

v2 changes no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog or wire protocol. Its only persistent effect is indirect, through the durability promise that CHECKPOINT_WAIT gives its callers, so this angle raises one objection. The xlog.h change is not described, so its ABI effect on extensions that pass CHECKPOINT_* flags could not be checked.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. It changes internal synchronization of shared-memory fields among server processes and adds no SQL surface, role, setting or monitoring view, and a correctness bug here is a concurrency matter for the design angle. The only user-visible change, a different error message in RequestCheckpoint, reveals nothing new to unprivileged users.
Objections given. Hot-path cost does not apply, because the touched paths are cold.
v2 uses the existing pg_atomic_uint32 and memory barriers rather than a new mechanism, and no extension or existing feature covers this; my objection applies only to v1 if it is still proposed.
One demand objection. v1 has the same gap across 20 files, and the thread does not say whether v1 is still proposed.
